## Introduction

\begin{block}{Literature Review}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Fires from Indonesia results in hazardous smoke spreading across the region, which pose significant environmental and public health threats.
  \item While traditional linear baselines struggle with non-linear time lags, machine learning algorithms account for these dynamics to improve air quality forecasts. 
\end{itemize}
\end{block}

\begin{block}{Research Objective}
To deploy and evaluate machine learning algorithms for forecasting haze levels in Singapore, providing actionable lead-time for public health planning.
\end{block}

\begin{block}{Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)}
Hourly regional observations reveal major mid-September surges exceeding 150 PSI, indicating macro-level pollutant drivers.
\end{block}

## Models
\begin{block}{Elastic Net}
Serves as our regularized linear baseline, efficiently managing severe multicollinearity across historical quality readings from different areas and weather factors. 
\end{block}

\begin{block}{Random Forest}
Non-linear ensemble of 500 trees forecasting west-region PSI at $t+1$ and $t+6$ hours. It can capture threshold effects that linear models miss, e.g. wind speed needing to exceed a critical value before smoke travels inland.
\begin{itemize}
  \item Predictors: PSI of all 5 regions (lags 0--5 h), wind vectors, Sumatra and Kalimantan fire power and counts, smoke-transport term.
  \item \texttt{mtry} chosen by out-of-bag (OOB) error.
  \item Time-based split: train 1 Aug--10 Oct, test 11--31 Oct 2019.
  \item Permutation importance (\%IncMSE), grouped by driver type.
\end{itemize}
\end{block}

## Random Forest: What Drives the Forecast?
\begin{columns}[T]
\begin{column}{0.52\textwidth}
\centering
\textbf{Top 15 predictors}\\[0.3em]
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{importance_plot.png}
\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.44\textwidth}
\centering
\textbf{Share of importance by group}\\[0.3em]
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{group_plot.png}
\end{column}
\end{columns}

\begin{block}{Findings}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{$t+1$:} most important predictors are the latest PSI readings across all regions (local persistence and spatial neighbours).
  \item \textbf{$t+6$:} fire power, hotspot counts and north--south wind move up the ranking, so upstream burning and transport matter more as the horizon grows.
  \item Higher importance does not mean better forecasts: the daily fire features may not generalise to the test period.
\end{itemize}
\end{block}

## Models (cont.)
\begin{block}{Vector Autoregressive Exogenous (VARX) System}
Models all 5 Singapore regions simultaneously ($\mathbf{Y}_t$) with wind vectors and Sumatra fire advection ($\mathbf{X}_t$)[cite: 3, 6]:
\begin{itemize}
  \item IRFs reveal that smoke entering the South region takes 2-3 hours to diffuse inland across neighbouring regions.
  \item Final model effectively tracks overall trends, but predictions are over-smoothed and show lag during sudden pollution spikes.
\end{block}


## Models (cont.)
\begin{block}{Spatial Autoregressive (SAR)}
Forecasts PM$_{2.5}$ across five Singapore regions while accounting for
spatial dependence between neighbours.
\[
\mathbf{y}_{t+h}=\rho_h W\mathbf{y}_{t+h}
+X_t\boldsymbol{\beta}_h+\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}_{t+h},
\quad h\in\{1,6\}.
\]
\begin{itemize}
  \item $W$: row-standardised neighbour weights; $\rho_h$: spatial dependence.
  \item $X_t$: current local PM$_{2.5}$, wind components, Sumatra fire power
        and region indicators.
  \item Fit by maximum likelihood; compare with OLS using RMSE and MAE
        across all regions on 21--31 October 2019.
\end{itemize}
\end{block}

\begin{block}{Conformal Coverage}
input 
\end{block}

## Results and Conclusion
\begin{block}{Evaluation of Models}
\centering
\begin{small}
```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
model_summary <- tibble(
  Model = c("Elastic Net", "Random Forest (t+1)", "Random Forest (t+6)", "VARX", "SAR (t+1)", "SAR (t+6)"),
  RMSE = c(5.67, 6.72, 10.10, 11.17, 5.78, 8.74),
  MAE  = c(4.57, 5.56, 8.54, 8.97,  4.43, 6.93),
  "R²"  = c(0.683, 0.620, 0.165, 0.031, 0.623, 0.179)
)

knitr::kable(
  model_summary,
  format = "latex",
  booktabs = TRUE,
  escape = FALSE,
  linesep = "",
  align = c("l", "c", "c", "c"),
  col.names = c("Model", "RMSE", "MAE", "R²")
)
```
\end{small}
\end{block}
\begin{block}{Results}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Top Model:} \textbf{Elastic Net} achieves the best forecasting performance, yielding the lowest test RMSE ($5.67$) and highest $R^2$ ($0.683$).
  \item \textbf{Non-Linear Advantage:} Captures complex lag dynamics and peak smoke surges much better than linear models (RF VS Elastic Net \& VARX).
  \item \textbf{Spatial Effects:} SAR model proves significant cross-boundary diffusion during the Southwest Monsoon.
  \item \textbf{Horizon Decay:} Accuracy drops at longer lead times ($t+6$) due to high atmospheric volatility and environmental uncertainty (RF \& SAR).
\end{itemize}
\end{block}
